subtype: Stage 2: Counting the roads not taken [Actor]
passage: Jeevan cut the motor at the canal and sat on the bund while the water spread slowly across the paddy. Twenty-five, he thought, and still in these fields. The bus to Mysuru passed on the road above, the same bus his classmate Rashmi had taken six years ago to join her nursing course. She had begged him to apply with her. He hadn't, because Appa's knee was bad and Amma cried at the thought of him leaving. Then there was the electronics diploma he dropped after one term, and the girl from the next village he never spoke to properly because his uncles were always watching. He counted them on muddy fingers: the course, Rashmi's bus, the girl, the lost year. Only the last felt like his own laziness. The rest had been decided by fear of disappointing someone, and that made them sting more, not less.

qa.q: Why didn't Jeevan apply with Rashmi?
qa.a: Because Appa's knee was bad and Amma cried at the thought of him leaving.

qa.q: Why do the chances decided by fear sting Jeevan more than the lost year?
qa.a: He feels those choices were never truly his; they were made to avoid disappointing others, so they carry regret and a sense of lost freedom.

qa.q: What could help Jeevan at this stage of counting losses?
qa.a: Sorting which chances are truly gone from those he could still revisit, and talking honestly with Amma and Appa about what he wants, could give the regret somewhere to go.

qa.q: How might Amma see Jeevan staying on the farm?
qa.a: Amma may see it as her son staying close and safe, without knowing how much he gave up to spare her tears.

grounding: Illustrates counting the roads not taken, where regret is sharpest for choices shaped by family worry and fear rather than desire.

passage:
The branch office pantry was empty at 7:40, and Nilesh was writing on the back of a deposit slip.

Architecture entrance, 2017. Didn't sit it. Papa said engineers get jobs.
Sukanya. Let her go to Pune without saying anything.
2020. Whole year on a coaching course I hated.

Gautam came in for the kettle and read it over his shoulder before Nilesh could fold it. "What's this, a confession?"

"Just a list." Nilesh's ears went hot. "Things I didn't do."

"Why now?"

Nilesh shrugged. The reunion photos last week, maybe. Or the way the sketchbook at the back of his cupboard had started to feel like a stranger's.

"The architecture one," Gautam said slowly, "that one wasn't really your choice, na?"

Nilesh looked at the slip. The first line was the one he'd written hardest, the pen almost through the paper. He didn't answer. He put the slip in his shirt pocket and went to open the counter.

qa.q: What was the first item on Nilesh's list?
qa.a: Architecture entrance, 2017, which he didn't sit because Papa said engineers get jobs.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when Gautam read the list?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and exposed, and underneath there was a deep regret, especially about the architecture choice he had written hardest.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Nilesh at this stage?
qa.a: He could talk honestly with Gautam or someone close about which items on the list still matter to him, instead of silently carrying the regret in his pocket.

qa.q: How might Gautam see Nilesh differently after this morning?
qa.a: Gautam may realise his colleague carries old disappointments behind the counter, and seems to understand that family pressure, not desire, shaped the biggest one.

grounding: In a workplace pantry, a person lists lost chances, with the sharpest regret tied to a choice made under family pressure.

subtype: Stage 2: Counting the roads not taken [Actor]
passage:
Subject: The list I've been making

Hi Nazia,

You asked last month why I've been so quiet. Here's the honest version.

I've been making a list. Late at night, mostly.

The Kathak diploma I dropped in Class 11 because Ma said dance was a hobby, not a future.
Rehaan, who asked me to come to Bengaluru with him, and I said no because I couldn't imagine telling my parents.
The gap year I wanted after graduation, which turned into a bank exam I didn't want and didn't clear.

What gets me is not that I chose wrong. It's that I don't think I chose at all. I chose whatever would make the least noise at home. I was scared, and I called it being sensible.

I'm not asking you to fix it. I just needed someone to read it who knew me back then.

Love,
Sonali

qa.q: Why did Sonali drop the Kathak diploma?
qa.a: Sonali dropped it because Ma said dance was a hobby, not a future.

qa.q: How can you tell Sonali's regret is tangled up with feeling afraid?
qa.a: Sonali writes that each choice was made to keep things quiet at home, and admits being scared and calling it being sensible.

qa.q: What small step would help Sonali now?
qa.a: Talking it through with Nazia, who knew Sonali back then, could help sort which of these lost chances can still be picked up in some form, like dance classes, and which need grieving.

qa.q: If you were Nazia reading this, what would you want?
qa.a: You might feel moved and a little sad for your friend, and you would want to call or meet soon to listen, since Sonali said this is not a request to fix things.

grounding: An email lists lost chances and shows how regret sharpens when choices were driven by family pressure and fear rather than desire.

subtype: Stage 2: Counting the roads not taken [Actor]
passage:
Arnab, you asked what I'm thinking about lately. Honestly? The year I lost.

I'm Sharmila, twenty-five, a pharmacist, which sounds fine, right? But when I was eighteen I wanted to study history. I'd got a seat. My uncle said history was for people who want to be poor, and Baba agreed, and I sat a full year of medical coaching instead. I failed the entrance. Then pharmacy, because it was close.

I keep going back to that year. I count it like money I dropped. I also count the old friend I stopped calling during it, and the photography club I quit because there was no time.

The funny thing is, I like my work sometimes. But when I pass the university gate on the bus, my stomach turns over. It wasn't the failing. It's that nobody asked me what I wanted, including me.

qa.q: Which subject did Sharmila want to study at eighteen?
qa.a: Sharmila wanted to study history.

qa.q: What does Sharmila's stomach turning at the university gate suggest?
qa.a: It suggests a sharp, lingering regret and sadness, tied less to failing and more to never being asked what Sharmila wanted.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Sharmila at this stage?
qa.a: Sharmila could start separating what still matters, such as history or photography, from the lost year itself, and explore small ways to bring those back.

qa.q: How might Arnab be affected by hearing this?
qa.a: Arnab asked out of concern and may feel trusted and a bit saddened, seeing a friend who seemed settled carrying a quiet ache.

grounding: A spoken account lists roads not taken, with regret sharpened because a family pushed the choice rather than the person's own desire.

One: music college in Chennai, the audition he'd passed at eighteen and never took up, because Appa said engineers eat and musicians starve. Two: Nisha, who'd moved to Mumbai, and whom he'd never told how he felt.
Thursday: at lunch in the office canteen, he added a third: the year after college he'd spent preparing for an exam he didn't even want. He read the list three times, feeling sick.
The next Monday: Sachin called to ask why he'd left the gig early. Madhav admitted, "Watching you play, I kept thinking, that could have been me. And I didn't even choose not to. I just did what I was told, or what felt safe." Sachin was quiet, then said, "You still play, though. Your guitar's in the corner of your room."
